chapter_theme: The ripe (பக்குவன்): the worthy disciple seeks a flawless guru, gives him goods, body and life, and stays at his feet like a shadow; sattvic, fearing birth, discerning the real from the unreal and melting in devotion, he receives the guru's foot and the knowledge it brings, and the teaching is to be given to such as he alone.
structure_note: The ripe seeker and his prayer (1690 to 1695), the marks of the true disciple, each verse ending in சற்சீடன் (1696, 1697, 1702, 1703), and between them the foot-initiation and how the teacher teaches (1698 to 1701).

1690.reading: The wise who worship, with scripture as their eye, know the flawless supreme guru; those who know the way are those who know the good way, and the others know only ruin.
1690.nuance: கருதி is taken as ச்ருதி, the revealed scripture, so scripture is the eye by which the true guru is recognised. அழிவறிவார் may mean they come to ruin.

1691.reading: Seeking you, Supreme One, I have stopped my trembling and given that up; from now I will join no one else; shatter the deeds of me your servant so that my thinking ends; kick me, my master, and take me gladly into your grace.
1691.nuance: The verse is a prayer, the only one in the chapter in the first person. உதைத்து (kicking) may recall Siva's foot that kicked Death, or the guru's foot placed on the disciple in initiation (1698); the plain sense is a plea to be taken by force.

1692.reading: Even while one trembles, the seed called the Supreme can be given to devoted singers by one who, looking from above at the sowing of the seed, sets their scattering minds straight.
1692.nuance: பரம் என்னும் வித்தை may be read as 'the knowledge (வித்தை, vidya) called the Supreme' or 'the seed called the Supreme', and the verse may play on both. Who gives is not named; the guru is implied.

1693.reading: If you take one, take a good guru; give him the goods you have, your body and your life; stand without break even for a sesame seed's while and know clearly: that is Siva's state itself.
1693.nuance: உள்ள பொருள் உடல் ஆவி (goods, body, life) is the classic threefold self-offering to the guru in Saiva tradition. The verse makes unbroken attention, not the gift alone, the way to Siva's state.

1694.reading: Jyoti, Visakha, then the two stars of the Scorpion and the Crab: to all but those who keep uprightness within justice, thinking the named day is when one comes to know, he knows neither the Primal nor anything.
1694.nuance: The first line names lunar asterisms (சோதி is Svati) and signs, perhaps days thought fit for initiation. The verse may be setting the upright mind above the auspicious day, or prescribing those days; the grammar of lines 2 to 4 is unclear.

1695.reading: When the Lord, for its beauty, takes his place in a mind made pure like a great jewel polished by work, deeds strong as weeds depart and one sees his anklet-bearing holy feet, and grace comes.
1695.nuance: தொழிலார மாமணி, a gem made bright by the jeweller's work, implies effort in purifying the mind. விழலார் விறலாம் வினை (deeds with the strength of weeds) is my reading of an unclear phrase.

1696.reading: He who, being sattvic, thinks on the supreme tattva, comes forth on the path of the faithful, fears the binding round of births, and can keep to the way of dharma: he is the true disciple.
1696.nuance: சாத்திகன் is one in whom the quality of sattva rules. ஆத்திக பேத நெறி (the path of the distinctions of belief) is unclear: perhaps the graded paths of the believer as against the unbeliever.

1697.reading: He who considers how the real and the unreal stand, melts his mind, bows when Siva's grace points the way so as to gain knowledge through devotion, and whose desire is fit for the Shakti of bliss: he is the true disciple.
1697.nuance: சத்து and அசத்து are taken in Siddhanta as the Lord (real) and the bonds (unreal), with the soul between. The verse joins discernment, devotion (பத்தி) and knowledge in one disciple.

1698.reading: 'Place your foot on me and grant grace': thinking of this, the teacher places his foot; the deceptive birth of the great head on which the foot is placed ends, and through the gracious Shakti of that body he who has received the foot becomes a knower free of fault.
1698.nuance: அடிவைத்து (placing the foot) opens every line. It is traditionally read as the guru's initiation by touch of the foot on the head (திருவடி தீக்கை). Lines 2 and 3 are compressed and my joins are guesses; ஆசு அற்றுளோன் is read as 'free of fault'.

1699.reading: As the desire for glorious knowledge grows and grows and a love that never came before turns to the supreme guru, he in whom the four means not yet possessed have come becomes a seeker of knowledge, fit for the foot to be placed on him.
1699.nuance: சாதகம் நான்கு may be the four qualifications of Vedanta (discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues, longing for release) or the four Siddhanta paths; the verse does not say. அடிவைக்கவே ties the verse to the foot-initiation of 1698.

1700.reading: Teach only those of ripe mind; setting them within the bound of the Supreme beyond, and facing east, south, north and west, teach them while meditating on the Lady of the tongue.
1700.nuance: நாவுடையாள் may be the goddess of speech or Shakti as the power of the word. The four directions may refer to the seating for initiation or to teaching in every quarter; பராபரத்து எல்லை is unclear.

1701.reading: When the disciple bows at the Lord's feet with the fivefold salutation, tells his want and praises with good heart, the one who shows him how to be rid of the prison of the body and makes knowledge known to the knower, together with Siva, is the follower of the true way.
1701.nuance: ஐ வணக்கம் may be the five-limbed prostration or simply 'the salutation'. சன்மார்க்கி (one on the true way) seems to name the teacher; the verse could also be read of the disciple. சிறையுடல் makes the body a prison.

1702.reading: Since Vedanta is the path of giving up desire, the one who turns aside the stream of worldly life and bows his head to the feet of the great Vedantin who gives up desire in Siddhanta is the true disciple.
1702.nuance: Tirumular joins the two: the teacher is a Vedantin whose renunciation is grounded in Siddhanta (சித்தாந்தத்து). வாழ்க்கைப் புனல் (the flood of worldly life) is to be diverted, not dammed.

1703.reading: Good quality, truth, compassion, discernment and gentleness, never leaving the true guru's feet, like a shadow, and gaining clear sight so that the supreme knowledge of consciousness is clear and wonder appears: such is the true disciple.
1703.nuance: The list of virtues (சற்குணம், வாய்மை, தயா, விவேகம், தண்மை) is ethical before it is spiritual. The shadow at the feet is the disciple's closeness; அற்புதம் (wonder) is the dawning of the supreme knowledge.

links.note: Both use the shadow that clings to the feet and never leaves: in the Kural it is the ruin that follows the evildoer, in Tirumular the true disciple's place at the guru's feet.

1823 calls the body the Lord's temple for those who have seen clearly; 1701 calls it a prison the teacher shows the disciple how to escape. The two can stand together if the body is a prison to the unreleased and a temple to the knower, but the images pull apart.

1690 says those who worship (தொழுதறிவாளர்) are the ones who know the flawless guru and the good way, while the rest know only ruin (அழிவறிவார்). Kural 2 asks what learning yields if the learned do not bow at the good feet of the pure knower (நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). Both make worship the test of knowledge; Tirumular adds scripture as the eye (கருதி கண்ணாக) and the guru as the one to be known.

In 1691 the speaker vows to join no one else (இனி யாரொடுங் கூடேன்) and asks the Lord to kick him and gladly take him (உதைத்து உடையாய் உகந்து ஆண்டருளாயே). Song 447 asks Murugan, so that the poet bows to no one else and does not aim at worldly ties (செகத்தோர் பற்றைக் குறியாதே), to set his flower feet on him and rule him (மலர்த்தாள் வைத்து ... ஆள்வாய்). Both join turning from all others to a plea to be ruled through the Lord's foot.

1691 has the devotee stop his trembling (பதைதொழிந்தேன்) before he asks to be taken. 1692 answers that even while one trembles (பதைக்கின்ற போதே) the seed called the Supreme can be given to devoted singers, once the teacher sets their scattering mind straight (சிதைக்கின்ற சிந்தையைச் செவ்வே நிறுத்தி). Read together, the end of trembling is not a condition of receiving the seed but something the giver brings about.

Kural 34 makes a spotless mind (மனத்துக்கண் மாசிலன் ஆதல்) the whole of virtue. 1695 takes the pure mind further: polished like a great gem by work (தொழிலார மாமணித் தூய்தான சிந்தை), it is where the Lord takes his place, and then deeds fall away and his feet are seen. The Kural's end becomes Tirumular's precondition for grace.

1696's true disciple thinks on the supreme tattva (பர தத்துவம் உன்னி) and fears the binding round of births (ஆர்த்த பிறவியின் அஞ்சி). Kural 358 calls birth a folly (பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை) that departs when one sees the true thing (செம்பொருள் காண்பது). Both tie the escape from birth to fixing the mind on the highest reality; Tirumular adds that the seeker must also keep to dharma (அறநெறி சாத்தவல்லான்).

Kural 351 says inglorious birth comes from taking what is not real as real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும் மருள்). 1697 makes the first mark of the true disciple that he considers how the real and the unreal stand (சத்தும் அசத்தும் எவ்வாறென), and then joins that discernment to devotion and grace. The Kural names the error; Tirumular builds the cure into the disciple's training.

1697 starts the disciple with weighing the real and the unreal (சத்தும் அசத்தும்). 1431 describes those who have passed beyond the real and the unreal (சத்தும் அசுத்துந் தணந்தவர்) and sink into the Shakti of bliss. Together they give the beginning and end of the same road: discrimination first, then a state where the distinction no longer holds; 1697's 'Shakti of bliss' (ஆனந்தச் சத்தி) is the very place 1431 ends.

1698 describes the teacher placing his foot (அடிவைத்து) on the disciple's head, so that deceptive birth ends and he becomes a knower free of fault. In 2433 the Lord set his foot on the poet's head (கால்கொண்டு என் சென்னியில்) so that his bonds were cut again and again and his delusion cut. Both make the foot on the head the act that undoes bondage; 2433 speaks it as experience, 1698 as the rule of initiation.

1698 sets out the guru's initiation by placing his foot on the head (அடிவைத்த மாமுடி). In song 1219 Arunagiri asks Murugan to drive off his impurity with Siva's light and set the paired feet on his head (எனது முடிமேலே இணைதாள் அளித்து), then grant him the teacher's place. The same rite of the foot on the head passes from Tirumular's account of the guru to a devotee's plea to Murugan as guru.

1699 says that as the desire for knowledge grows and an unprecedented love turns to the supreme guru (வாராத காதல் குருபரன் பாலாக), the seeker becomes fit for the foot to be placed on him. In 1590, as love rose (இசைந்தெழும் அன்பில்), the guru came and placed his hand on the poet's head. Both make the disciple's rising love the sign that the guru's touch is due; 1699 states it as a qualification, 1590 as an event.

1700 tells the teacher to teach only those of ripe mind (மதிபக்குவர்க்கே உணர்த்தி). Kural 720 says that speaking before those not of one's own kind is nectar spilled in a dirty yard (அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்தற்றால்). Both hold that teaching is wasted on the unfit; Tirumular makes ripeness the measure where the Kural speaks of the hearers' group.

1702 calls Vedanta the path of giving up desire and makes the true disciple one who bows to a Vedantin grounded in Siddhanta (சித்தாந்தத்து ... வேதாந்தி). 2393 states the doctrine behind this: becoming Siva is both Vedanta and Siddhanta, and apart from that each is in vain (அவம் அவம் ஆகும்). 1702 shows the joined teaching embodied in a single teacher.
